incidents.cause: Total loss of engine power during the agricultural application flight for reasons that could not be determined.
The pilot’s delay in releasing product to reduce the airplane’s weight and improve its climb performance, which was reduced because of the high density altitude.
Separation of the No. 3 cylinder exhaust valve rocker arm, which resulted in a loss of engine power.
The total failure of a cylinder head assembly. Contributing to the accident was the lack of suitable terrain for a forced landing.

The engine failure due to several loose, damaged cylinder stud nuts and hold-down bolts. Contributing to the accident was maintenance personnel’s failure to detect that the cylinder nuts and hold-down bolts were not properly secured during the engine’s most recent inspection.
The partial loss of engine power due to a fatigue failure of the engine cylinder exhaust rocker housing as a result of an excessively torqued rocker assembly.

The oil filler cap not reinstalled by the pilot prior to the aerial application flight and the total loss of engine oil during an aerial application. Additional causes were the low altitude of the operation and the unsuitable terrain encountered by the pilot during the forced landing.
The pilot's failure to maintain aircraft control.  Contributing factors were the high temperature and tailwind.

A partial loss of engine power due to the failure of two compressor turbine blades as a result of the engine operating near or above the engine’s operating limits for an undetermined amount of time beyond the recommended engine’s TBO limit, which led to material creep and overload failure.
A total loss of engine power due to a cracked No. 2 cylinder head.
Loss of engine power for undetermined reasons.
A partial loss of engine power for undetermined reasons which led to a forced landing in unsuitable terrain.
The partial loss of engine power for reasons that could not be determined during postaccident examinations.
A partial loss of engine power while maneuvering at low altitude due to a failure of the airplane’s supercharger.
The pilot’s failure to set the engine speed control fully forward during takeoff, resulting in an engine surge and subsequent loss of control during landing.
Maintenance personnel’s improper installation of the left magneto, which resulted in oil starvation to the engine and a subsequent total loss of engine power.
The pilot’s controlled flight into terrain likely due to spatial disorientation, while flying over sparsely lighted terrain at night.

The noninstrument-rated pilot’s improper decision to depart in dark, night marginal visual flight rules conditions, which resulted in his spatial disorientation and subsequent loss of airplane control.
Fatigue failure of the nose wheel fork, which resulted in separation of the nose wheel.
A partial loss of engine power due to lose baffling from the muffler, which resulted in an obstruction of the exhaust system.
An in-flight collision with a bird during initial climb.

The pilot’s geographic disorientation while maneuvering in the airport traffic pattern in dark night conditions, which resulted in the airplane descending below a normal approach path and a collision with trees. Contributing to the accident was the pilot's lack of recent night flight experience.

incidents.op: CAE OXFORD AVIATION ACADEMY PHOENIX INC
incidents.cause: A coyote strike and the subsequent operation of the airplane, which led to internal composite wing structure damage.
The flight instructor’s inadequate supervision and delayed remedial action during an unusual attitude recovery, which resulted in a descent into terrain.

The pilot’s decision to continue visual flight into deteriorating weather, which resulted in an encounter with instrument meteorological conditions and subsequent inability to maintain clearance with terrain.
The pilot's inadequate takeoff performance planning, which resulted in collision with an obstacle during takeoff from a turf runway that was not long enough for the given conditions.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control on landing roll out.
The student pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the landing, and the flight instructor’s inadequate remedial action.
The pilot's failure to properly maintain the airplane and engine, which resulted in a total loss of engine power due to improperly installed magnetos and a broken camshaft.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during a wheel landing in crosswind conditions and the flight instructor’s delayed remedial action, which resulted in a ground loop on the runway.
The pilot's selection of an unsuitable landing surface, which resulted in a loss of control during the landing roll.
The overstress fracture and failure of a main landing gear wheel during landing, resulting in the right wing striking the ground.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the takeoff, which resulted in a runway excursion.
A total loss of engine power during cruise flight due to the failure of the crankshaft gear.

The airplane’s failure to climb at a sufficient rate to clear trees and terrain beyond the end of the runway for reasons that could not be determined because postaccident examination did not reveal any mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation.
The pilot's misjudgment of the speed and distance required to land, which resulted in a runway overrun.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll with a left crosswind.

The uncertificated pilot’s decision to fly an unairworthy airplane and his failure to maintain directional control during landing, which resulted in a landing gear collapse. Contributing was the failure of the right main landing gear oleo strut.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control while landing in variable wind conditions, which resulted in runway excursion and collision with an approach light.
A loss of engine power for an undetermined reason.
The total loss of engine power after takeoff for undetermined reasons.
A rapid throttle advancement after a period of idling, which resulted in a flooded engine and total loss of engine power.
The mechanic's improper installation of the turbocharger assembly, which resulted in oil starvation and a subsequent total loss of the engine power.
The pilot’s loss of visual reference during the landing approach which resulted in a collision with water.
A separation of the window from the airframe for undetermined reasons.
An environmental stress cracking failure of the acrylic windshield, which resulted in a rapid decompression during cruise flight.
Brake application before all three landing gears were on the ground, which caused the failure of the right main landing gear tires and resulted in tire fragments impacting the fuselage.
Overheated brakes due to the extended taxi at a higher power setting in an attempt to burn off fuel to achieve the proper takeoff weight that resulted in a wheel fire during takeoff.
An inadvertent encounter with convectively induced turbulence (CIT) during descent.
A No. 1 (left) engine fire due a fuel leak that originated from the fuel nozzle 17 b-nut connection that was not properly torqued in accordance with the aircraft maintenance manual procedure.

The flightcrew’s misidentification of the intended landing runway, which resulted in approach to and landing on the wrong runway. Contributing to the incident was the distraction caused by the dual reset of the flight management computer displays.
